explainedBy: Comparison: L'Enfant points at the third path (the park) while the council man stares blankly past it: the binary blinded them.

storyboard.claim: Locked in the binary, the council ignored L'Enfant's third option, the park.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Fork-in-the-road icon with the dotted third path; L'Enfant points at it, the alderman blank.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the critique of the either-or to the option they missed.
storyboard.addedInformation: The third path is literally drawn as the road they did not take.

explainedBy: Event: L'Enfant's plan was built in Washington and the capital still stands shaped by it.

storyboard.claim: In Washington, L'Enfant's vision was implemented and the National Mall still shapes the capital.
storyboard.concreteVisual: L'Enfant points proudly at an intact city.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrast: where his vision was built, it lasted.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the proof case: the same architect's plan, realized.

explainedBy: Cause -> effect: the narrow framing led to the pond being buried under rock instead of becoming a lasting park.

storyboard.claim: Collect Pond could have been New York's Boston Common, but once buried under rock it is gone.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow diagram builds: Narrow framing -> Pond buried.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Starts the cause chain of the Collect Pond lesson.
storyboard.addedInformation: The chain from framing to the buried pond is laid out.

explainedBy: Cause -> effect completed: narrow framing -> pond buried -> it can never come back; irreversibility is what makes the framing deadly.

storyboard.claim: The irreversibility of the choice is what makes narrow framing deadly.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same flow gains its third label: Never get it back.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept flow; adds the irreversible result.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the 500-year mistake / house / company examples stay in the audio.

explainedBy: Comparison: instead of the two obvious roads, the listener points to the third path: widen the map before choosing.

storyboard.claim: Don't pick between the two obvious paths; resist resolving the tension fast and widen the map first.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener points at the fork icon's third dotted path.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the 1802 case to the advice for the listener.
storyboard.addedInformation: Applies the third-option icon to the viewer's own decision.

explainedBy: Darwin in his study holds the notebook with the two-column list, trying to resolve his tension over marriage.

storyboard.claim: Back to Darwin in his smoky room, resolving his own tension in a notebook.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Darwin, worried, holds his notes beside the two-column list icon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to the opening case.
storyboard.addedInformation: Re-establishes Darwin and his two-column list.

explainedBy: Under Marry he writes a wife would be better than a dog: the dog is drawn as the thing he compares her to.

storyboard.claim: Under Marry: a nice soft wife on a sofa, better than a dog anyhow.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Darwin keeps his notes; the dog icon replaces the list.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept Darwin; the icon changes to the dog he names.
storyboard.addedInformation: The dog literally shows the comparison he wrote.

explainedBy: Commentary: his bar for marriage is set at the warmth a dog gives; the dog stays beside him.

storyboard.claim: As romance, this leaves much to be desired: the bar is basic mammalian warmth.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Darwin with the dog still beside him, now just talking.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; his smirk drops to a plain face.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the joke is carried by the hosts' words.

explainedBy: Another entry on the Marry side: the charms of music and conversation; he smiles over the list.

storyboard.claim: He also lists the charms of music and female chit-chat.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Darwin smiles, the two-column list back on screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept Darwin; back to the list, face happy.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks this as one more pro in the left column.

explainedBy: Change: he turns to the Not Marry column and the anxiety pours out; his face falls over the list.

storyboard.claim: In the Not Marry column the anxiety pours out: fatness, idleness, expense.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Darwin slumps, worried, over the same list.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept list; the face turns from happy to worried.
storyboard.addedInformation: The switch from pros to cons is shown as a change of mood over the same page.

explainedBy: More cons: the expense of children and missing the conversation of clever men at clubs; he is sadder still.

storyboard.claim: He fears the expense of children and losing the conversation of clever men at clubs.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Darwin sad, slumped over the list.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept list; worried -> sad.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the specific con is named by the callout.

explainedBy: His biggest fear on the list: a wife who dislikes London would banish him to the countryside; he is afraid.

storyboard.claim: He is terrified a wife who dislikes London would banish him to the countryside, idle.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Darwin afraid, clutching his notes by the list.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept list; the face peaks at fear.
storyboard.addedInformation: The fear is shown on his face, the cause in the label.

callout.text: Fears on a scrap of paper

explainedBy: Summary: he is putting his fears and hopes onto the paper he holds, making the abstract concrete.

storyboard.claim: He is externalizing his fears and hopes on a scrap of paper.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Darwin calm again, holding the notes beside the list.
storyboard.onScreenText: Fears on a scrap of paper
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept list; fear settles into a neutral face, the paper holds it now.
storyboard.addedInformation: The paper in hand is the point: the list externalizes the feelings.

explainedBy: Origin: the two-column method goes back to Benjamin Franklin writing a letter in 1772; Franklin holds the letter.

storyboard.claim: The two-column method has a pedigree going back to Franklin's 1772 letter.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Franklin holds a letter in his study.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: New case: the method's origin.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces Franklin and the letter that carries the method.

explainedBy: Relationship: the letter's recipient is Franklin's friend Joseph Priestley, the scientist who discovered oxygen.

storyboard.claim: Franklin wrote to his friend Joseph Priestley, who discovered oxygen.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Priestley in front, Franklin beside him with a friendly face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the recipient of the letter.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: oxygen itself cannot be drawn; the label carries it.

explainedBy: Priestley, briefcase in hand, slumps worried over a big career decision.

storyboard.claim: At the time, Priestley was agonizing over a massive career decision.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Priestley alone, worried, holding a briefcase.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Focus moves to Priestley's dilemma.
storyboard.addedInformation: The briefcase marks the choice as a job decision.

explainedBy: The offer: a prestigious post as librarian to the Earl of Shelburne; he holds a book, still worried about uprooting his family.

storyboard.claim: Whether to uproot his family to become librarian and companion to the Earl of Shelburne.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Priestley, still worried, now holds a book.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept Priestley; the briefcase becomes a book (the librarian post).
storyboard.addedInformation: The book names the job on offer.

explainedBy: Relationship: paralyzed Priestley asks for advice; Franklin, letter in hand, answers not what to choose but how to process the choice.

storyboard.claim: Paralyzed, Priestley asked Franklin; Franklin answered he could not say what to choose, only how to process the choice.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Franklin joins, holding the letter out; Priestley slumped and worried.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept room; Franklin enters with his reply.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows who advises whom.

explainedBy: Hand-over: Priestley takes Franklin's letter as Franklin outlines his system, 'moral algebra'.

storyboard.claim: Franklin outlines a system he calls moral or prudential algebra.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Priestley takes the letter from Franklin's outstretched hand.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept pair; the letter passes from Franklin to Priestley.
storyboard.addedInformation: The hand-over shows the method traveling in the letter.

explainedBy: Mechanism step one: take a sheet, divide it into two columns, write pros and cons; the two-column page appears beside Priestley reading the letter.

storyboard.claim: Franklin told Priestley to divide a sheet into two columns of pros and cons.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Priestley holds the letter; the two-column list icon appears.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept Priestley holding the letter; the method itself appears.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the exact layout the letter prescribes.

explainedBy: Contrast: the modern listener knows the list but has forgotten Franklin's second step; he holds the page blankly.

storyboard.claim: Everyone knows the list, but society has forgotten the crucial second step.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The modern listener with notes, blank, beside the list.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Franklin's era to today's half-remembered method.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: forgetting is carried by the blank face and the label.

explainedBy: Mechanism: write the list, then let it sit a few days for the subconscious to work.

storyboard.claim: Step two: after writing the list, let it sit for a few days.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow: Write the list -> Let it sit.
storyboard.onScreenText: Write the list -> Let it sit
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Starts drawing Franklin's procedure as steps.
storyboard.addedInformation: The forgotten step is shown in its place in the sequence.

explainedBy: Mechanism continued: come back and weigh the items by their relative importance.

storyboard.claim: Then you return and weigh each item's relative importance.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The flow gains a third step: Weigh the items.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept flow; adds step three.
storyboard.addedInformation: Completes the three-step procedure.

explainedBy: Mechanism: one pro equal to two cons balances out, so all three are struck; Franklin points to the scale.

storyboard.claim: If one pro equals two cons, strike all three out.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Franklin points at a balance scale.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From steps to how weighing cancels items.
storyboard.addedInformation: The scale shows equal weights cancelling.

explainedBy: Same rule again: two pros equal to three cons cancel, cross all five out.

storyboard.claim: Two pros equal to three cons: cross all five out.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Franklin, pleased, keeps the scale.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept scale; second example of the rule.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the numbers ride on the label.

explainedBy: Result of the mechanism: keep balancing until a surplus remains on one side of the scale.

storyboard.claim: You balance the equation algebraically until a surplus remains on one side.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Franklin now holds the notes by the scale.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept scale; Franklin takes up the page to finish the sums.
storyboard.addedInformation: Ties the algebra to the paper list.

explainedBy: Result: the items left uncrossed on the two-column list are taken as the correct choice.

storyboard.claim: Whatever remains standing is the 'objectively correct' choice; now to the real world.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The two-column list alone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: End of the method: the list decides.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the 'objectively' irony is left to the hosts.

explainedBy: Event: the listener is handed a big job offer from a competitor; he takes the offer letter at midnight.

storyboard.claim: Imagine you've just been handed a massive job offer from a competitor; it's midnight.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener takes an offer letter, surprised, in the kitchen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Franklin to a modern listener at a crossroads.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the trigger of the decision as an event.

callout.text: The old job or the new one

explainedBy: Structure: on the legal pad the left column is 'current job', the right column 'new job'.

storyboard.claim: At the kitchen table you write 'current job' on the left, 'new job' on the right.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A two-bucket sorter: Current job | New job.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The listener sets up Franklin's two columns.
storyboard.addedInformation: The columns are named as the narration names them.

explainedBy: Weighing: the 30% salary bump on one side against the 45-minute longer commute on the other; the listener holds the pad by the scale.

storyboard.claim: You weigh the 30% salary bump against a 45-minute longer commute, the title against your friend.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener with the legal pad beside a balance scale.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From columns to weighing items.
storyboard.addedInformation: Pairs the two items on a scale.

explainedBy: Weighing continues: the new title against leaving your work best friend; his face falls.

storyboard.claim: The prestigious title weighs against leaving your work best friend; you do the Franklin algebra.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same scale; the listener slumps, sad.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept scale; the face turns sad at the personal cost.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the emotional item on the scale.

explainedBy: Result: the salary outweighs the commute, he crosses it out and arrives at a 'mathematical' answer.

storyboard.claim: You cross out the commute because the salary is so good and reach a mathematical answer.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same scale; the listener happy with his pad.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept scale; sad -> relieved at the answer.
storyboard.addedInformation: Ends the worked example with its verdict.

explainedBy: Commentary: the host learned this two-column list from his dad on a legal pad when choosing a college.

storyboard.claim: The host loves the method; his dad taught him the legal-pad list when picking a college.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The two-column list icon alone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shift from example to personal endorsement.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the dad and college are in the audio only.
